Neonatal common mole-rats (Cryptomys hottentotus) are extremely altricial at parturition, with a wet weight at birth of 8.0 grams [Wwb = 8.0 grams], reflecting the limited maternal investment typical of this subterranean, cooperatively breeding bathyergid. This modest mass is consistent with values reported for other small-bodied Cryptomys species and underscores the high degree of offspring dependency. Newborns are naked, blind, and entirely dependent on maternal care within the natal burrow. The ultrastructure of the placenta is well-suited to support rapid foetal growth, yet the birth mass is constrained by the energetic demands of a pregnant female inhabiting an energetically costly subterranean environment. The gestation period, which lasts 81 days [tg = 81 days] at the typical colony temperature of 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C], is relatively protracted for a rodent of this size, and has been attributed to the low metabolic rates and stable thermal conditions of the species' underground habitat. This extended gestation may facilitate the delivery of a relatively precocial newborn compared to other altricial rodents, although the neonate mass remains low in absolute terms. The interplay between gestation length and birth mass is a key component of the species' conservative life-history strategy in a resource-limited environment.

The nursing period in Cryptomys hottentotus is marked by continuous maternal provisioning and is heavily influenced by the stable thermal microenvironment of the colony. Under the constant temperature regime maintained within the burrow system, 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C], the age since birth at weaning is 82 days [tx = 82 days]. This extended suckling phase is associated with the gradual transition from milk to solid food, a process assisted by the transfer of partially digested plant matter from colony members. At the point of nutritional independence, the wet weight at weaning is 26.1 grams [Wwx = 26.1 grams], a substantial increase from the birth mass but still far below the adult size, indicating that significant post-weaning growth is required. The weaning body mass is critical because it represents the threshold at which the young individual becomes capable of independent foraging on the geophytes and underground storage organs that dominate the species' diet. The duration of the weaning period is likely correlated with colony size, as older siblings may contribute to provisioning, thereby reducing the direct energetic burden on the lactating female.

Growth continues steadily following weaning, and the ultimate or asymptotic wet weight of the common mole-rat is 67 grams [Wwi = 67 grams]. This ultimate wet weight, which represents the maximum adult body mass attained after somatic growth has ceased, is reached gradually during the prolonged juvenile and sub-adult phase. The attainment of this asymptotic mass is a notable milestone because it coincides with the transition from a strictly non-reproductive colony role to potential breeding status. The species exhibits a pronounced reproductive skew, with only a single dominant female per colony typically attaining full reproductive capacity. The other colony members, both male and female, remain reproductively suppressed while they continue to contribute to burrow maintenance and foraging. The ultimate body mass is relatively large compared to some solitary bathyergids, a feature linked to the behavioural dominance hierarchy that characterises this species' cooperative breeding system. The 67 grams [Wwi = 67 grams] adult mass provides the necessary reserves to sustain the high energetic costs of gestation and lactation for the breeding female.

The most common mole-rats also display a delayed pattern of sexual maturation, consistent with their social structure and extended lifespan. In captive colonies maintained at a constant 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C], the age since birth at puberty is 450 days [tp = 450 days]. The onset of gonadal activity is tightly regulated by social cues, primarily the presence of a breeding queen, through pheromonal suppression. In the absence of a dominant breeding female, subordinate females may attain reproductive capability earlier, though 450 days [tp = 450 days] appears to be a baseline under stable social conditions. at a temperature of 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C]The relatively late age at sexual maturity, compared to similar-sized rodents, is associated with the species' extended lifespan. Their maximum recorded lifespan under favourable conditions is 11 years [am = 11 years], which provides a long reproductive window for the breeding individual at a temperature of 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C]. This longevity of 11 years is remarkable for a small mammal and is thought to be facilitated by the protection of the subterranean niche from predators and climatic extremes, as well as the extended period of social care afforded to the queen by non-breeding colony members.

Reproductive output in Cryptomys hottentotus is carefully regulated, with the dominant female typically producing a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year] at a colony temperature of 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C]. Litter size is small, averaging 8 pups per litter [N_R_i = 8 pups per litter], and given the annual breeding frequency of one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], the maximum reproductive rate is low, constituting approximately 8 pups per year [Ri = approximately 8 pups per year]. This conservative strategy is typical of K-selected species inhabiting stable but resource-limited environments, where parental investment per offspring is high. The maximum reproductive rate is further constrained by the extended duration of both gestation and lactation, which together span over 163 days of direct maternal investment. The low annual reproductive outputnan is offset by high offspring survival within the protected colony environment, where predation is minimal and cooperative care improves the nutritional status of young. When combined with the species' extended maximum lifespan, this modest annual fecundity yields a surprisingly high lifetime reproductive output for the colony queen. The shared thermal regime of 34.4 °C underpins all these developmental and reproductive parameters, highlighting the importance of stable burrow temperatures for this species' unique life-history evolution among rodents.
